# The Compass and the Storm

Ekin had been standing at the harbour stall for a full minute, turning the brass compass over in her palms, when the shadow fell across her. It came from above and behind, fast and silent, and by the time she looked up, a broad-bodied dragon, no taller than Ekin's waist, had landed on the pier, its tail curling around the stall's post. Its wings were folded like a grey cloak, its belly wide and pale, and it didn't roar or breathe fire at all. It simply leaned down, its long neck stretching over her shoulder, and plucked the compass from her hands with two neat claws, and the short braided cord that had been looped around her wrist snapped and stayed behind.

"Hey—that's mine!" Ekin grabbed at empty air. The dragon's wing swept backward as it turned, knocking a stack of paper receipts off the stall and scattering them across the wet stone like startled gulls. The fishmonger swore and ducked. The dragon paid no attention to any of it. It lifted the compass to its eye, tilted its head as if admiring the shine, and then launched itself off the pier with three powerful wingbeats.

Ekin ran. The dragon rose, banked, and she lost it against the bright grey sky, her heart hammering. She spun around, searching the rooftops, the masts, the breakwater—then a voice behind her said, "You're going the wrong way. The lighthouse."

She turned. A girl her own age stood there, arms crossed, dark hair whipping in the wind. Ekin had seen her around the harbour before but had never spoken to her.

"It went toward the cliffs," Ekin said.

"It went toward the lighthouse." The girl pointed. "See the window? There's a glint in it. Metal catches the light."

Ekin squinted. High on the old lighthouse's seaward face, in a broken upper window, something flashed—brief, brass-bright, gone.

"That's my grandfather's compass," Ekin said. "He used to take me out along the coast with it. I was just looking at it. That dragon just—"

"Took it. Yes." The girl was already walking, briskly, toward the path that climbed the headland. "Are you coming or not?"

Ekin hesitated for one breath, then ran to catch up.

"I'm Duru, by the way," the girl said, without looking back. "This is the coast path. Stay on it."

The path ran above the tide line, dry and sheltered, winding along the shoulder of the headland toward the lighthouse. Below it, the shore was a chaos of wet stone and rock pools, and it looked shorter—Ekin could see the lighthouse directly across the jumble of rocks.

"The shore's faster," she said.

"The shore's where the waves will be in half an hour." Duru nodded at the horizon, where a wall of dark cloud had begun to lean against the sky. The wind had picked up since the harbour, and whitecaps were showing far out. "Look at the tide line on those rocks. See the dark stain? The water reaches there when it blows from the west. That's where we're standing if we go down."

Ekin looked. The stain was high—higher than she'd guessed. She felt a small, stubborn itch to argue anyway, just because Duru had said it like a teacher, but the wind chose that moment to shove her sideways, and she decided the path was fine. It was fine.

They climbed in a rattling silence broken by Duru pointing things out despite herself: the old anchor chain half-buried in the grass, the hollow where fishermen used to dry their nets. "Nobody's been up to the lighthouse in years," Duru said. "The keeper moved to the mainland. But the door—"

"The door's open," Ekin said.

It stood in the tower's seaward wall, a heavy iron-banded thing, ajar for the first time in what looked like a very long while. Sand and gull feathers had drifted across the threshold. A smell came out of the dark inside—salt, and something warmer, like sun-baked stone.

Duru stopped with her hand on the door. "I always wanted to see inside," she admitted, quietly, as if confessing to something.

"Then let's go," Ekin said, and slipped past her through the opening.

Inside, the door opened straight onto a broad room, cold air and drifting light. Daylight poured through a wide broken window, and the room was dry, bright, littered with old machinery and dust. And in the far corner, heaped against the wall beneath the broken glass, was the dragon.

The room was bigger than Ekin had expected, and stranger. The wind moaned through the broken window in low, shifting notes, like someone humming behind a closed door. The glass in the remaining panes had gone cloudy with salt, so the light came through thick and pearly. Old winch gears stood along one wall under shrouds of dust, and every bright thing in the room had been collected into one corner: a brass ship's bell, a lantern with a polished reflector, a handful of doorknobs, a tin lid, a fisherman's lucky coin, all piled in a wide, shallow nest of dried grass and rope ends.

And on top of the pile, unmistakable, lay the compass.

Ekin's chest tightened. There it was—her grandfather's compass, dented at the edge where she'd once dropped it, the needle casing fogged with salt from a hundred mornings at the shore. The dragon was curled around the nest, its body filling the whole corner, its head resting on its forelegs. Its eye was open. It was watching them.

"Don't move yet," Duru whispered.

"Why not—"

"Because of that." Duru pointed, very slightly, with her chin.

Ekin followed her look and saw it: a small shape at the edge of the nest, hardly bigger than a cat, peering out from behind its mother's wing. A hatchling—sleek, grey-green, with enormous eyes and a damp, unfinished look about it, the way kittens have. It was nudging at the tin lid with its nose, utterly absorbed.

"It's a baby," Ekin breathed.

"And the mother is between us and the whole room," Duru said. "So we wait. We watch. We don't walk up to a dragon's nest and grab things, even if—"

But Ekin had already stopped listening, because one of the dragon's wings had shifted, just an inch, and beneath it she could see the compass's brass edge catching the pearly light. Every hiss and rustle from the mother felt aimed at her, like a dare. Duru wasn't the boss of this. It was her compass. Her grandfather's.

She noticed, distantly, a narrow doorway in the far wall, and a staircase corkscrewing down into the dark of the tower's lower floor. From somewhere below came the sound of waves—close, hollow, drumming against stone. The sea was already speaking through the building.

"Wait," Duru said again, sharper now.

Ekin didn't.

She crossed the room in six quick strides and reached for the compass.

The mother came off the nest like a door slamming. One wing flared wide, wider than Ekin's outstretched arms, and the hiss that came out of the animal was pure fury and pure warning all at once, and Ekin stumbled backward, her hand never touching the brass. The compass, knocked by the edge of the wing, rolled off the nest, bounced once on the stone floor, and skittered to the narrow doorway, where it tipped over the top step and went clattering down the narrow corkscrew stairs, bouncing from step to step until it landed on the floor of the lower room.

The hatchling shrieked, a sound like a kettle coming to the boil, and bolted. Ekin saw it go—saw it pour itself down the same narrow staircase in a tumble of claws and tail, vanishing round the turn of the stair and into the lower dark after a hiding place only it knew. The mother lunged after it, got her head and shoulders into the stairwell, and jammed. Her chest was simply too broad for the turning stair. She shoved, wings battering the doorframe, dust and grit raining down, and got nowhere. She was stuck, half-in, half-out, hissing down into the dark where her baby had gone.

"She can't fit," Duru said. She had not moved from her spot, and her voice was tight. "The stairs turn too tight. She can't follow it down."

"Then I'll—"

"No." Duru caught her arm. "Wait. Look."

Ekin leaned into the stairwell, peering down the spiral. The little stair was short, one tight spiral that opened onto the lower room; from the upper turn she could see down into the gloom, where the compass lay on the stone floor near the seaward wall—and beyond the compass, a wide opening in that wall, closed by a fixed iron grille, and beyond the grille, the sea. The waves were no longer drumming from a distance. They were coming through. White water surged against the bars, and spray was already spitting through the gaps, wetting the floor in a growing, creeping sheet.

A swell surged harder than the rest. Water foamed through the grille, rushed across the floor, and dragged the compass with it. Ekin watched it scrape over the stone, catch for one horrible half-second on the bars, and then slide through the gap and out, into the grey churn, gone. Only the cord, still hanging from her wrist where it had snapped at the harbour, was left to her.

"No," she said. "No, no—"

Below, the hatchling scrambled up onto a dry stone ledge at the foot of the stairs, only a few steps below the turn, out of the water's reach, and pressed itself there, shivering, its eyes two dots of reflected white.

The wind rose. The waves rose. The mother, wedged in the stairwell above them, hissed down into the dark at her baby, at the water, at everything, and could do nothing at all.

For a long moment Ekin couldn't look away from the grille. The compass was out there, somewhere under the grey water, and her whole body wanted to run down those stairs and find some way—any way—to get it back.

"We have to go," Duru said. "The water's coming up. This whole floor will be under it."

"But it's right there—"

"It's gone, Ekin. It's in the sea."

Ekin knew it. She could see it. Some stubborn part of her refused to accept it, and that part was shouting down every other thought. Then the hatchling cried out again—small, high, desperate—from its ledge, and the mother thrashed against the doorframe above, and Ekin felt something in her chest turn over.

"I scared it," she said. Her voice came out flat and strange. "It ran because of me. It's down there because of me. The compass too—if I hadn't lunged at it—"

"Yes," Duru said. She didn't soften it and she didn't pile on. She just said it, and then she said: "So what are you going to do?"

Ekin looked at the stairs, at the hatchling on its ledge, at the water climbing the floor below in slow, glittering advances. She thought about the dry room above, and the open door, and the path home, and how easy it would be to just leave. To run. The compass was lost either way.

"Help me," she said.

Duru's jaw was set and her eyes were angry, and she stayed. "The ledge near the bottom is still dry," she said. "If it comes to the stairs, we can get it up."

Ekin went down. The steps were dry all the way down the spiral; the water had not reached them. She crouched on the lowest dry step, a few steps above the ledge, opened her jacket, and held it out—not toward the hatchling, not chasing it, just open, like a nest, like a suggestion. The hatchling pressed itself back against the stone, hissing, its whole small body shaking.

"I know," Ekin said softly. "I know. I'm the one who scared you. I'm sorry."

Behind and above her, Duru stood one step higher, watching the lower room over Ekin's shoulder, calling the water level: "Still dry. Still dry. Coming up on the left—move your foot." Her voice steadied Ekin more than she could say.

The swell came, and the ledge began to vanish under the foam, and the hatchling had nowhere left to retreat except toward the stairs—toward Ekin. It hesitated, trembling. Ekin didn't grab. She waited, jacket open, heart pounding, and the wave decided for all of them: the hatchling sprang up the last steps, landed against her chest, and burrowed into the jacket like it had always lived there.

Ekin rose, one hand cupping the small warm weight, and climbed the same steps back up. Duru took her arm on the upper steps, steadied her, and pulled her through the doorway into the dry light of the upper room. The mother was already off the stairwell, wings wide, and Ekin walked straight to her and knelt and let the hatchling tumble out of her jacket onto the nest.

The mother's head came down over her baby. The hiss this time was low, and brief, and ended.

Ekin backed away, slowly, and the dragon let her. She stood beside Duru in the middle of the room, wind howling through the broken window, and watched as the mother folded herself around the hatchling, one great wing drawing over it like a roof. The dragon did not speak. It did not nod or thank them. It did not reach into the nest and bring out a gift, and Ekin understood, in a way that settled into her bones, that it never would. The hatchling peeked out from under the wing once, looked at her with its enormous eyes, and tucked itself back in.

It wasn't obedience, exactly. It was just that Duru was right, and Ekin could admit it now.

They walked a while in the rain's soft noise. Duru didn't mock her about the compass, and somehow that was worse and better than teasing all at once.

"It's really gone," Ekin said at last.

"Yes."

"I keep thinking I'll see it on the beach tomorrow. Washed up. But I won't, will I."

"No."

Ekin's hand was in her pocket, where she had tucked the short braided cord from her wrist when they left the tower—a cord with nothing on the end of it now. She wound it around her fingers, once, twice, feeling the emptiness of it, and found that she didn't want to hide it or lie about what had happened. She would tell her grandfather the truth. The dragon took it, and then I lost it, and then I left it in the sea, and here's what came back instead of it. She let the cord go slack again.

Duru had drawn a few steps ahead, her shoulders hunched against the rain. Ekin had fallen behind without noticing. She did not call out to her, and Duru did not turn around to hurry her.

The loss was still there, as heavy as the wet air, and the quiet between them did not pretend otherwise. But something had changed between them since the harbour. Ekin could feel it, and it did not undo the loss. It simply sat beside it.

The harbour lights were coming into view below. She wound the cord around her fingers once more. Then she let it go.

Ahead, the path curved down toward the harbour lights, and the rain kept falling; Ekin turned the empty cord over in her pocket, and hurried to catch up.

spans: Ekin had been standing at the harbour stall for a full minute, turning the brass compass over in her palms, when the shadow fell across her.
It came from above and behind, fast and silent, and by the time she looked up, a broad-bodied dragon, no taller than Ekin's waist, had landed on the pier, its tail curling around the stall's post.
Its wings were folded like a grey cloak, its belly wide and pale, and it didn't roar or breathe fire at all.

It simply leaned down, its long neck stretching over her shoulder, and plucked the compass from her hands with two neat claws, and the short braided cord that had been looped around her wrist snapped and stayed behind.
"Hey—that's mine!" Ekin grabbed at empty air.
The dragon's wing swept backward as it turned, knocking a stack of paper receipts off the stall and scattering them across the wet stone like startled gulls.
The dragon paid no attention to any of it.
It lifted the compass to its eye, tilted its head as if admiring the shine, and then launched itself off the pier with three powerful wingbeats.
The dragon rose, banked, and she lost it against the bright grey sky, her heart hammering.
She spun around, searching the rooftops, the masts, the breakwater—then a voice behind her said, "You're going the wrong way.
A girl her own age stood there, arms crossed, dark hair whipping in the wind.
Ekin had seen her around the harbour before but had never spoken to her.
"It went toward the cliffs," Ekin said.
"It went toward the lighthouse." The girl pointed.
High on the old lighthouse's seaward face, in a broken upper window, something flashed—brief, brass-bright, gone.
"He used to take me out along the coast with it.
I was just looking at it.
Yes." The girl was already walking, briskly, toward the path that climbed the headland.
Ekin hesitated for one breath, then ran to catch up.
"I'm Duru, by the way," the girl said, without looking back.
The path ran above the tide line, dry and sheltered, winding along the shoulder of the headland toward the lighthouse.
Below it, the shore was a chaos of wet stone and rock pools, and it looked shorter—Ekin could see the lighthouse directly across the jumble of rocks.
"The shore's where the waves will be in half an hour." Duru nodded at the horizon, where a wall of dark cloud had begun to lean against the sky.
The wind had picked up since the harbour, and whitecaps were showing far out.
"Look at the tide line on those rocks.
The water reaches there when it blows from the west.
That's where we're standing if we go down."
The stain was high—higher than she'd guessed.
She felt a small, stubborn itch to argue anyway, just because Duru had said it like a teacher, but the wind chose that moment to shove her sideways, and she decided the path was fine.
They climbed in a rattling silence broken by Duru pointing things out despite herself: the old anchor chain half-buried in the grass, the hollow where fishermen used to dry their nets.
"Nobody's been up to the lighthouse in years," Duru said.
It stood in the tower's seaward wall, a heavy iron-banded thing, ajar for the first time in what looked like a very long while.
Sand and gull feathers had drifted across the threshold.
A smell came out of the dark inside—salt, and something warmer, like sun-baked stone.
Duru stopped with her hand on the door.
"I always wanted to see inside," she admitted, quietly, as if confessing to something.
"Then let's go," Ekin said, and slipped past her through the opening.
Inside, the door opened straight onto a broad room, cold air and drifting light.
Daylight poured through a wide broken window, and the room was dry, bright, littered with old machinery and dust.
And in the far corner, heaped against the wall beneath the broken glass, was the dragon.
The room was bigger than Ekin had expected, and stranger.
The wind moaned through the broken window in low, shifting notes, like someone humming behind a closed door.
The glass in the remaining panes had gone cloudy with salt, so the light came through thick and pearly.

Old winch gears stood along one wall under shrouds of dust, and every bright thing in the room had been collected into one corner: a brass ship's bell, a lantern with a polished reflector, a handful of doorknobs, a tin lid, a fisherman's lucky coin, all piled in a wide, shallow nest of dried grass and rope ends.
And on top of the pile, unmistakable, lay the compass.
There it was—her grandfather's compass, dented at the edge where she'd once dropped it, the needle casing fogged with salt from a hundred mornings at the shore.
The dragon was curled around the nest, its body filling the whole corner, its head resting on its forelegs.
"Because of that." Duru pointed, very slightly, with her chin.
Ekin followed her look and saw it: a small shape at the edge of the nest, hardly bigger than a cat, peering out from behind its mother's wing.
A hatchling—sleek, grey-green, with enormous eyes and a damp, unfinished look about it, the way kittens have.
It was nudging at the tin lid with its nose, utterly absorbed.
"And the mother is between us and the whole room," Duru said.
We don't walk up to a dragon's nest and grab things, even if—"
But Ekin had already stopped listening, because one of the dragon's wings had shifted, just an inch, and beneath it she could see the compass's brass edge catching the pearly light.
Every hiss and rustle from the mother felt aimed at her, like a dare.
Duru wasn't the boss of this.
She noticed, distantly, a narrow doorway in the far wall, and a staircase corkscrewing down into the dark of the tower's lower floor.
From somewhere below came the sound of waves—close, hollow, drumming against stone.
The sea was already speaking through the building.
She crossed the room in six quick strides and reached for the compass.
The mother came off the nest like a door slamming.

One wing flared wide, wider than Ekin's outstretched arms, and the hiss that came out of the animal was pure fury and pure warning all at once, and Ekin stumbled backward, her hand never touching the brass.

The compass, knocked by the edge of the wing, rolled off the nest, bounced once on the stone floor, and skittered to the narrow doorway, where it tipped over the top step and went clattering down the narrow corkscrew stairs, bouncing from step to step until it landed on the floor of the lower room.
The hatchling shrieked, a sound like a kettle coming to the boil, and bolted.
Ekin saw it go—saw it pour itself down the same narrow staircase in a tumble of claws and tail, vanishing round the turn of the stair and into the lower dark after a hiding place only it knew.
The mother lunged after it, got her head and shoulders into the stairwell, and jammed.
Her chest was simply too broad for the turning stair.
She shoved, wings battering the doorframe, dust and grit raining down, and got nowhere.
She was stuck, half-in, half-out, hissing down into the dark where her baby had gone.
She had not moved from her spot, and her voice was tight.
Ekin leaned into the stairwell, peering down the spiral.

The little stair was short, one tight spiral that opened onto the lower room; from the upper turn she could see down into the gloom, where the compass lay on the stone floor near the seaward wall—and beyond the compass, a wide opening in that wall, closed by a fixed iron grille, and beyond the grille, the sea.
The waves were no longer drumming from a distance.
White water surged against the bars, and spray was already spitting through the gaps, wetting the floor in a growing, creeping sheet.
A swell surged harder than the rest.
Water foamed through the grille, rushed across the floor, and dragged the compass with it.
Ekin watched it scrape over the stone, catch for one horrible half-second on the bars, and then slide through the gap and out, into the grey churn, gone.
Only the cord, still hanging from her wrist where it had snapped at the harbour, was left to her.

Below, the hatchling scrambled up onto a dry stone ledge at the foot of the stairs, only a few steps below the turn, out of the water's reach, and pressed itself there, shivering, its eyes two dots of reflected white.
The mother, wedged in the stairwell above them, hissed down into the dark at her baby, at the water, at everything, and could do nothing at all.
For a long moment Ekin couldn't look away from the grille.
The compass was out there, somewhere under the grey water, and her whole body wanted to run down those stairs and find some way—any way—to get it back.
This whole floor will be under it."
Some stubborn part of her refused to accept it, and that part was shouting down every other thought.
Then the hatchling cried out again—small, high, desperate—from its ledge, and the mother thrashed against the doorframe above, and Ekin felt something in her chest turn over.
Her voice came out flat and strange.
It's down there because of me.
The compass too—if I hadn't lunged at it—"
She didn't soften it and she didn't pile on.
She just said it, and then she said: "So what are you going to do?"
Ekin looked at the stairs, at the hatchling on its ledge, at the water climbing the floor below in slow, glittering advances.
She thought about the dry room above, and the open door, and the path home, and how easy it would be to just leave.
The compass was lost either way.
Duru's jaw was set and her eyes were angry, and she stayed.
"The ledge near the bottom is still dry," she said.
"If it comes to the stairs, we can get it up."
The steps were dry all the way down the spiral; the water had not reached them.
She crouched on the lowest dry step, a few steps above the ledge, opened her jacket, and held it out—not toward the hatchling, not chasing it, just open, like a nest, like a suggestion.
The hatchling pressed itself back against the stone, hissing, its whole small body shaking.
I'm the one who scared you.
Behind and above her, Duru stood one step higher, watching the lower room over Ekin's shoulder, calling the water level: "Still dry.
Coming up on the left—move your foot." Her voice steadied Ekin more than she could say.
The swell came, and the ledge began to vanish under the foam, and the hatchling had nowhere left to retreat except toward the stairs—toward Ekin.

She waited, jacket open, heart pounding, and the wave decided for all of them: the hatchling sprang up the last steps, landed against her chest, and burrowed into the jacket like it had always lived there.
Ekin rose, one hand cupping the small warm weight, and climbed the same steps back up.
Duru took her arm on the upper steps, steadied her, and pulled her through the doorway into the dry light of the upper room.
The mother was already off the stairwell, wings wide, and Ekin walked straight to her and knelt and let the hatchling tumble out of her jacket onto the nest.
The mother's head came down over her baby.
The hiss this time was low, and brief, and ended.
Ekin backed away, slowly, and the dragon let her.
She stood beside Duru in the middle of the room, wind howling through the broken window, and watched as the mother folded herself around the hatchling, one great wing drawing over it like a roof.
It did not nod or thank them.
It did not reach into the nest and bring out a gift, and Ekin understood, in a way that settled into her bones, that it never would.
The hatchling peeked out from under the wing once, looked at her with its enormous eyes, and tucked itself back in.
They went back across the room, away from the narrow stair and the flooding room below it, to the door they'd come through, and out into the wind.
The coast path was still dry, still sheltered, though the sea below had climbed to its dark stain on the rocks and the rain was starting in slanting sheets.
At the fork where the path bent inland, she called back, "This way—the low ground floods," and Ekin followed without a word, without arguing, without even feeling the usual itch to.
It was just that Duru was right, and Ekin could admit it now.
They walked a while in the rain's soft noise.
Duru didn't mock her about the compass, and somehow that was worse and better than teasing all at once.
"It's really gone," Ekin said at last.
"I keep thinking I'll see it on the beach tomorrow.
Ekin's hand was in her pocket, where she had tucked the short braided cord from her wrist when they left the tower—a cord with nothing on the end of it now.
She wound it around her fingers, once, twice, feeling the emptiness of it, and found that she didn't want to hide it or lie about what had happened.
She would tell her grandfather the truth.
The dragon took it, and then I lost it, and then I left it in the sea, and here's what came back instead of it.
She let the cord go slack again.
Duru had drawn a few steps ahead, her shoulders hunched against the rain.
Ekin had fallen behind without noticing.
She did not call out to her, and Duru did not turn around to hurry her.
The loss was still there, as heavy as the wet air, and the quiet between them did not pretend otherwise.
But something had changed between them since the harbour.
Ekin could feel it, and it did not undo the loss.
The harbour lights were coming into view below.
She wound the cord around her fingers once more.
Ahead, the path curved down toward the harbour lights, and the rain kept falling; Ekin turned the empty cord over in her pocket, and hurried to catch up.

approved_plan.mock_context:
**Ekin:** On iki yaşında bir kız. Meraklı, çabuk karar veriyor; kendisine yol
gösterilmesini küçümsenmek gibi algılıyor. Dedesiyle yaptığı kıyı gezilerinden
kalan pirinç pusula, o gezileri tek başına da yapabileceğine dair kişisel bir
hatıra. Dedenin öldüğü varsayılmayacak; hikâye bir yas anlatısına dönüştürülmeyecek.

**Duru:** Ekin'in yaşıtı. Eski fenerin yolunu biliyor. Ekin'e hizmet eden kusursuz
yardımcı değil: laf sokuyor, merakını bazen saklıyor, kendi fikrinin dinlenmesini
istiyor. Fenerin kapısı uzun süredir ilk kez açık olduğu için o da içeri girmek
istiyor. Ortaklıklarının başlangıç nedeni yalnızca Ekin'e iyilik etmek değil.

**Anne deniz ejderhası:** Çocukların beline yaklaşan, geniş gövdeli bir hayvan;
diğer ejderhalara göre küçük. Uçabilir, küçük bir metal nesneyi taşıyabilir.
Konuşmaz, büyü yapmaz, insan niyetini okuyamaz. Yuvaya parlak eşyalar taşır.
İnsanlara saldırma amacı yok; yaklaşanı kanat açıp tıslayarak uzaklaştırır.

**Yavru:** Kedi büyüklüğünde, koşabilir ve dar aralıklara girebilir; henüz
uçamaz. Düşüp yaralanması veya grafik acı tasviri yok. Korktuğunda dar, karanlık
bir yere saklanma davranışı var. Annenin ganimetleriyle ilgilenmesi keşifte görülür.

**Başlangıç eşyaları:** Ekin'in pusulası ve ceketi; Duru'nun sıradan giysileri.
Sonradan ip, kanca, kesici alet, özel ışık veya kurtarma ekipmanı belirmeyecek.

alt deniz duvarına dahi ulaşmaz; çocuklar kısa bir ziyaret yapabileceklerini sanır.

geçemez. Bu engel sahnede annenin gerçekten denemesiyle görünür; sonradan ilan

Çocuklar yüzmeye, dalmaya veya görünmeyen zeminde ilerlemeyecek.

Duru dalgaların oraya kadar çıkacağını gösterir. Ekin onun yolunu isteksizce kabul

scenes.title: Geri dönmek yerine sorumluluk almak
scenes.approved_action:
Ekin önce gözünü pusulanın kaybolduğu ızgaradan ayıramaz. Duru gitmeleri gerektiğini
söyler; ardından yavrunun su yükseldikçe geri çekildiğini görürler. Ekin hayvanı
kendisinin ürküttüğünü kabul eder ve Duru'dan yardım ister. Duru da ona kızgın
olmasına rağmen kalır. Karar: Kendi kaybına kapanıp ayrılmak mı, yol açtığı
tehlikeyi gidermek için güvenli kalan kısa fırsatı kullanmak mı?

onu suya doğru kovalamaz. Duru aynı merdivende bir üst basamakta durur; görüşü
izler ve Ekin'in ceketle aldığı yavruyu yukarı aktarırken destek olur. Yavru
ulaşılabilir taş çıkıntıdadır; uçuruma atlama, suya dalma veya yeni büyü yoktur.
Ekin ardından aynı basamaklardan çıkar. Yazım bu basit eylemi sayfalar süren bir
mekanik bulmacaya çevirmemeli; gerilim Ekin'in tereddüdü ve hayvanın korkusundadır.
scenes.required_end_state: Çocuklar ve yavru kuru üst odada; anneyle buluşurlar. Pusula hâlâ kayıp.

# The Tide Thief

Ekin had been waiting all morning for the clouds to thin enough to read the sky, but the brass compass in her hands didn't care about clouds. Its needle swung once, steadied, and pointed her straight along the harbor wall toward the headland where the old lighthouse stood. Her grandfather had pressed it into her palm at the end of last summer, with the promise that she could come back and walk the coast on her own. This was supposed to be that walk.

The shadow crossed her before she heard the wings.

It dropped out of the low grey sky like a thrown cloak — a sea dragon, smaller than the ones fishermen grumbled about, but broad across the chest, with wings that caught the wind and snapped taut. Its claws closed around the compass cord, wrenched it free of her fingers, and beat upward in a single heavy stroke. The downdraft scattered a fishmonger's paperwork across the wet cobbles, and someone shouted as a stack of receipts swirled into the harbor.

"My compass!" Ekin was already running, boots skidding on the slick stones. "Come back — that's mine!"

The dragon didn't even look back. It rose over the roofs, banked once, and glided toward the headland.

Ekin cut left, toward the cliff steps that climbed the fastest way up, but a hand caught her sleeve.

"Not that way." A girl her own age stood there, dark hair whipped across her face, pointing with her chin. "It went to the Light. See?" In the lighthouse's highest window, something small and brass flashed once in the grey light. "Duru," the girl added, as if that explained everything. "I know those cliffs. You don't."

Ekin yanked her sleeve back, ready to argue, then looked at the cliff steps, at the wind flattening the grass up there, at the flash in the window again. The compass was her grandfather's. She wasn't leaving it in a dragon's nest.

"Fine," she said. "But I'm not waiting for you."

"Good," said Duru. "I wasn't going to wait either."

The coastal path left the harbor through a gap in the sea wall and climbed gently along the spine of the headland, well above the tideline. Duru walked it like she'd been born on it, stepping over the loose stones without looking down.

Ekin lasted about two hundred paces before the shortcut tempted her. "There." She pointed down the slope, where a rocky shelf of ledges angled toward the lighthouse's base. "That's half the distance."

"And half the air," Duru said. She stopped, crouched, and laid her palm flat on a dark stone near the path's edge. It glistened. "Feel that. The wind's turned, and when it turns, the swell comes up over those rocks." She nodded at a line of dried seaweed clinging to the boulders well above the water. "The sea left that there this morning. You want to be standing under it when the next wave remembers?"

Ekin looked. The waves were still slapping harmlessly against the lower sea wall, but the seaweed told a different story, and the wind was rising in longer, colder pulls. She hated being told what to do — hated it most when the person telling her was right.

"Fine," she muttered. "Your path."

"My path," Duru agreed, without any gloating in it, which somehow made it worse and better at the same time.

They climbed. Below them the harbor shrank to a scatter of masts; above them the lighthouse grew, its white paint gone grey and scabbed with salt. Ekin had never been this close. "Is it really empty?" she asked, breathing harder than she wanted to admit. "Everyone says it's been shut for years."

"Shut, yes," Duru said. "Empty —" She stopped at the bend where the path met the flat ground of the headland, and stared.

The lighthouse's upper door stood open. Not broken, not hanging off its hinges — just open, wide and dark, the first time in living memory.

"Nobody opens that door," Duru said quietly, and for the first time since the harbor, her voice carried no teasing at all. Just curiosity, sharp and bright.

They looked at each other. Whatever had stolen Ekin's compass had also opened a door that nobody opened, and neither of them could walk past that.

Ekin went in first. Duru followed, and pulled the door shut behind them against the rising wind — not locked, just closed, the way they'd found the way back clearly marked by the path outside the window. The room they stepped into was dry and tall, lit by a wide window on the seaward side whose glass had long ago cracked and fallen away, leaving a jagged, generous opening to the sky.

And in that opening, folding her wings like a ship coming to anchor, was the thief.

The mother dragon was smaller than the stories claimed sea dragons were, but she filled the corner of the room the way a boat fills a boathouse. She had woven her nest into the crushed shadow of the broken window out of whatever the sea and the wind had offered: coiled rope, torn fishing net, dried kelp, and — gleaming through it all like coins at the bottom of a well — a hoard of small bright things. A silver spoon. A brass door handle. A child's tin whistle. A pocket watch with no hands.

And there, resting on the very edge of the pile, its glass face catching the grey daylight: the compass.

Ekin's heart slammed. "There it is —"

"Wait." Duru's hand came out, not grabbing, just open, like a fence. Her eyes weren't on the nest. They were on the shadows behind it, where a shape the size of a large cat had uncurled — a hatchling, all oversized flippers and wet down, watching them with round dark eyes. "There's a baby. Don't go near it. Don't go near *any* of it. Mothers don't like —"

The mother dragon hissed. It wasn't a roar, nothing dramatic — just a long, dry, razor sound, and her wings half-opened, shading the nest like a drawn curtain. Between the children and the pile of treasure, she had settled herself like a wall.

Ekin heard the hiss and felt it land on her like a dare. *That's my compass. My grandfather's compass.* Every sound the dragon made seemed to say *no*, and every *no* made Ekin's jaw set harder.

"Keep your voice down," Duru whispered. "I'm not telling you what to do. I'm telling you what's true."

The wind moaned through the broken window, and beneath it, from somewhere below the floor, came another sound — rhythmic, heavy, hollow. Ekin glanced around and saw it: a narrow staircase spiraling down into the lighthouse's belly, human-sized, tight and turning, its stone steps worn smooth in the middle. The wave-sound rose from down there, muffled and enormous, the noise of the sea hitting something fixed and iron.

"The lower room," Duru breathed. "There's a grate down there, open to the water. This whole tower is a drum in a storm."

"Then we take the compass and go," Ekin whispered back, eyes fixed on the brass flash at the nest's edge. "It's right *there*."

The mother dragon watched them. The hatchling peeked around her flank. The waves boomed below, and the wind tore at the broken window, and the door behind them stayed exactly where they'd left it — shut, but not locked, the path home plain through the dry daylight outside.

Ekin didn't plan it. That was the thing she would turn over later, walking home — there had been no plan, just the compass sitting three steps away in a pile of stolen junk, and her hand already moving.

"I'm just taking what's mine," she said, and lunged.

The mother dragon moved faster than anything that broad had a right to. One wing snapped out, thick as a sail, and swept the air between them. Ekin flinched back — and the wind of the wing's passage, or the drag of her sleeve, or simply the whole room flinching with her, knocked the compass off the nest's edge.

It hit the floor with a brass clatter and rolled. Ekin dove, missed, and watched it spin in a widening arc across the floorboards, past her fingers, over the lip of the stairwell opening, and down — a shrinking spiral of flashing brass, ticking against every worn step, down and down into the drumming dark.

The hatchling shrieked — a thin, uncanny sound — and bolted after it, flippers scrabbling, vanishing down the same stairs in three bounds.

The mother roared and threw herself at the stairwell. She didn't fit. It was that simple and that terrible: her shoulders jammed against the curved stone at the first turn, her wings pinned half-folded, her claws scrabbling on rock as she heaved and wedged and could not pass. The whole tower shuddered. She backed out, hissing, jammed herself in again, and got no further.

"Duru — the compass —"

"I see it." Duru was flat on her stomach at the stairwell's lip, peering down. "It's stopped. There's a ledge — the little one's near it —" Then her face changed. "Ekin. The water."

Ekin crowded next to her. Far below, through the lower room's seaward opening, she could see it: a fixed iron grate, bars thick as her wrist, and beyond the bars the grey sea heaving. A wave struck the grate and burst through it, not as spray but as a whole moving wall, sweeping across the lower floor, slamming against the stair's stone base.

And when it drained back, the compass went with it — a small bright tumble through the bars, out into the churn, gone.

Ekin stared at the grate. The sea stared back, grey and vast and absolutely uninterested.

The hatchling, washed and terrified, hauled itself out of the reach of the next wave onto a dry stone ledge near the bottom of the stairs, pressed itself against the wall, and made itself small. Above, its mother thrashed once more against the stone turn of the stairwell, felt the shape of the passage with her snout, and went still — stuck on the wrong side of her own child's hiding place.

The wind rose. The waves came faster.

Ekin couldn't look away from the grate. The compass was down there — *had been* down there — and some stubborn part of her kept waiting for the sea to give it back, for a wave to set it gently on the stones like an apology.

"We have to go." Duru was on her feet. "The tide's still coming in. This room — the whole bottom of the tower —"

"I know." Ekin's voice came out flat. Her hands were fists. Her grandfather's compass, given with a promise, swallowed by the sea in front of her own eyes because she had lunged at a dragon's nest without thinking. "I know it's gone."

"Then let's —" Duru stopped. She was looking down the stairs again. "Ekin. The baby."

The water had reached the base of the ledge. The hatchling had retreated to the last dry handspan of stone and stood there shivering, too frightened to climb the steps toward the huge stuck shape of its mother, too crowded by the rising wash to stay.

Ekin looked at the lost compass. She looked at the hatchling. The choice arranged itself with brutal clarity: she could walk out the door with Duru right now and grieve properly, or she could go down those stairs and fix the thing she had broken.

"I scared it down there," she said. "It ran because of me." She swallowed. "I need your help. Please."

Duru looked at her for a long second — angry, Ekin could see, genuinely angry, and staying anyway. "The ledge holds for now," Duru said. "The steps above the wet line are dry. Go. I'll watch the water."

Ekin went down, step by careful step, on the dry upper stairs. At the level of the ledge she crouched, slowly, and opened her jacket, holding one side out like a sling.

"Hey," she said softly. "Hey. It's all right."

The hatchling hissed, a tiny copy of its mother's sound, and pressed harder into the corner.

"Don't corner it," Duru called down. "Don't reach over it. Let it come to you."

"I'm not going to chase you into the water," Ekin said. "I already did enough." She stayed exactly where she was, coat open, hand out, and waited. The hatchling's round eyes fixed on her. Below, the sea drew back for the next wave.

"Big one coming," Duru said. "Ekin."

"I know."

The hatchling took one shuffle-step toward her. Then another. Whether it was the cold, the noise, or the open coat that looked more like a nest than anything else in the tower, Ekin never asked. At the last moment, as the roar of the incoming wave filled the lower room, Ekin scooped — gently, under the belly, the way you'd lift a stray cat — and tucked the hatchling against her chest inside the jacket just as the water exploded against the grate below the ledge and swirled over the stone where it had been standing.

"Go!" Duru pulled her by the shoulder as she came up. Step by step, Ekin climbed, the hatchling a warm trembling weight against her ribs, Duru a half-flight above her calling out the dry steps, until they spilled together into the dry upper room, sea-damp and shaking, and Ekin knelt and let the hatchling spill out of her coat onto the floorboards.

The mother dragon was off the stairwell and across the room before it finished righting itself.

Ekin picked the hatchling up one last time — it had gone strangely still, watching its mother's face — and carried it the last few steps, setting it down right at the edge of the nest, close enough to touch. "Here," she said. "It's yours. It was always yours."

The mother dragon did not speak. She did not thank anyone, did not nod, did not return a brass button or a handless watch from her hoard, and did not produce a compass from anywhere. She lowered her head, touched her snout once to the hatchling's damp back, and then folded her wing over it completely, a great taut curtain of it, until only a small wet head peeked out between the feathers of her edge.

The storm had not stopped. The waves still boomed against the grate below, and the wind still tore at the broken window, and the lighthouse still drummed like a struck barrel. But the upper room was dry, and the door was still just a door.

They went out the way they'd come in — along the coastal path, above the seaweed line, the safe way Duru had shown her. When the path forked at the steep slope, Duru said, "Left here, above the black rocks," and Ekin turned left without a word, without checking the slope first, without needing to. Duru, for her part, said nothing about the compass at all. Nothing about the nest, or the lunging, or the sea. The loss sat between them, acknowledged, unmocked, and that was its own strange kindness.

By the time they came down into the harbor, the fishermen were restacking their scattered papers and the sky had gone the color of wet slate. Somewhere behind them, up on the headland, the storm went on without them.

Ekin's hand went to her pocket out of habit, into the space where the compass should have been — and found only the cord, the empty brass cord with its little clasp, which had somehow stayed looped through her belt loop when everything else had been swept away. She didn't hide it. She didn't tuck it away or pretend it wasn't there. She stood at the harbor wall for a moment, turning the empty cord slowly around her finger, feeling how light it was and how heavy.

Then she ran three quick steps and caught up with Duru, walking side by side into the wind.

She had woven her nest into the crushed shadow of the broken window out of whatever the sea and the wind had offered: coiled rope, torn fishing net, dried kelp, and — gleaming through it all like coins at the bottom of a well — a hoard of small bright things.
A silver spoon.
A brass door handle.
A child's tin whistle.
A pocket watch with no hands.
And there, resting on the very edge of the pile, its glass face catching the grey daylight: the compass.
Ekin's heart slammed.
"There it is —"
"Wait." Duru's hand came out, not grabbing, just open, like a fence.
Her eyes weren't on the nest.
They were on the shadows behind it, where a shape the size of a large cat had uncurled — a hatchling, all oversized flippers and wet down, watching them with round dark eyes.
"There's a baby.
Don't go near it.
Don't go near *any* of it.
Mothers don't like —"
The mother dragon hissed.
It wasn't a roar, nothing dramatic — just a long, dry, razor sound, and her wings half-opened, shading the nest like a drawn curtain.
Between the children and the pile of treasure, she had settled herself like a wall.
Ekin heard the hiss and felt it land on her like a dare.
*That's my compass.
My grandfather's compass.* Every sound the dragon made seemed to say *no*, and every *no* made Ekin's jaw set harder.
"Keep your voice down," Duru whispered.
"I'm not telling you what to do.
I'm telling you what's true."
The wind moaned through the broken window, and beneath it, from somewhere below the floor, came another sound — rhythmic, heavy, hollow.
Ekin glanced around and saw it: a narrow staircase spiraling down into the lighthouse's belly, human-sized, tight and turning, its stone steps worn smooth in the middle.
The wave-sound rose from down there, muffled and enormous, the noise of the sea hitting something fixed and iron.
"The lower room," Duru breathed.
"There's a grate down there, open to the water.
This whole tower is a drum in a storm."
"Then we take the compass and go," Ekin whispered back, eyes fixed on the brass flash at the nest's edge.
"It's right *there*."
The mother dragon watched them.
The hatchling peeked around her flank.

The waves boomed below, and the wind tore at the broken window, and the door behind them stayed exactly where they'd left it — shut, but not locked, the path home plain through the dry daylight outside.
Ekin didn't plan it.
That was the thing she would turn over later, walking home — there had been no plan, just the compass sitting three steps away in a pile of stolen junk, and her hand already moving.
"I'm just taking what's mine," she said, and lunged.
The mother dragon moved faster than anything that broad had a right to.
One wing snapped out, thick as a sail, and swept the air between them.
Ekin flinched back — and the wind of the wing's passage, or the drag of her sleeve, or simply the whole room flinching with her, knocked the compass off the nest's edge.
It hit the floor with a brass clatter and rolled.

Ekin dove, missed, and watched it spin in a widening arc across the floorboards, past her fingers, over the lip of the stairwell opening, and down — a shrinking spiral of flashing brass, ticking against every worn step, down and down into the drumming dark.
The hatchling shrieked — a thin, uncanny sound — and bolted after it, flippers scrabbling, vanishing down the same stairs in three bounds.
The mother roared and threw herself at the stairwell.
She didn't fit.

It was that simple and that terrible: her shoulders jammed against the curved stone at the first turn, her wings pinned half-folded, her claws scrabbling on rock as she heaved and wedged and could not pass.
The whole tower shuddered.
She backed out, hissing, jammed herself in again, and got no further.
"Duru — the compass —"
"I see it." Duru was flat on her stomach at the stairwell's lip, peering down.
"It's stopped.
There's a ledge — the little one's near it —" Then her face changed.
"Ekin.
The water."
Ekin crowded next to her.
Far below, through the lower room's seaward opening, she could see it: a fixed iron grate, bars thick as her wrist, and beyond the bars the grey sea heaving.
A wave struck the grate and burst through it, not as spray but as a whole moving wall, sweeping across the lower floor, slamming against the stair's stone base.
And when it drained back, the compass went with it — a small bright tumble through the bars, out into the churn, gone.
Ekin stared at the grate.
The sea stared back, grey and vast and absolutely uninterested.
The hatchling, washed and terrified, hauled itself out of the reach of the next wave onto a dry stone ledge near the bottom of the stairs, pressed itself against the wall, and made itself small.
Above, its mother thrashed once more against the stone turn of the stairwell, felt the shape of the passage with her snout, and went still — stuck on the wrong side of her own child's hiding place.
The wind rose.
The waves came faster.
Ekin couldn't look away from the grate.
The compass was down there — *had been* down there — and some stubborn part of her kept waiting for the sea to give it back, for a wave to set it gently on the stones like an apology.
"We have to go." Duru was on her feet.
"The tide's still coming in.
This room — the whole bottom of the tower —"
"I know." Ekin's voice came out flat.
Her hands were fists.
Her grandfather's compass, given with a promise, swallowed by the sea in front of her own eyes because she had lunged at a dragon's nest without thinking.
"I know it's gone."
"Then let's —" Duru stopped.
She was looking down the stairs again.
"Ekin.
The baby."
The water had reached the base of the ledge.

The hatchling had retreated to the last dry handspan of stone and stood there shivering, too frightened to climb the steps toward the huge stuck shape of its mother, too crowded by the rising wash to stay.
Ekin looked at the lost compass.
She looked at the hatchling.
The choice arranged itself with brutal clarity: she could walk out the door with Duru right now and grieve properly, or she could go down those stairs and fix the thing she had broken.
"I scared it down there," she said.
"It ran because of me." She swallowed.
"I need your help.
Please."
Duru looked at her for a long second — angry, Ekin could see, genuinely angry, and staying anyway.
"The ledge holds for now," Duru said.
"The steps above the wet line are dry.
Go.
I'll watch the water."
Ekin went down, step by careful step, on the dry upper stairs.
At the level of the ledge she crouched, slowly, and opened her jacket, holding one side out like a sling.
"Hey," she said softly.
"Hey.
It's all right."
The hatchling hissed, a tiny copy of its mother's sound, and pressed harder into the corner.
"Don't corner it," Duru called down.
"Don't reach over it.
Let it come to you."
"I'm not going to chase you into the water," Ekin said.
"I already did enough." She stayed exactly where she was, coat open, hand out, and waited.
The hatchling's round eyes fixed on her.
Below, the sea drew back for the next wave.
"Big one coming," Duru said.
"Ekin."
"I know."
The hatchling took one shuffle-step toward her.
Then another.
Whether it was the cold, the noise, or the open coat that looked more like a nest than anything else in the tower, Ekin never asked.

At the last moment, as the roar of the incoming wave filled the lower room, Ekin scooped — gently, under the belly, the way you'd lift a stray cat — and tucked the hatchling against her chest inside the jacket just as the water exploded against the grate below the ledge and swirled over the stone where it had been standing.
"Go!" Duru pulled her by the shoulder as she came up.

Step by step, Ekin climbed, the hatchling a warm trembling weight against her ribs, Duru a half-flight above her calling out the dry steps, until they spilled together into the dry upper room, sea-damp and shaking, and Ekin knelt and let the hatchling spill out of her coat onto the floorboards.
The mother dragon was off the stairwell and across the room before it finished righting itself.

Ekin picked the hatchling up one last time — it had gone strangely still, watching its mother's face — and carried it the last few steps, setting it down right at the edge of the nest, close enough to touch.
"Here," she said.
"It's yours.
It was always yours."
The mother dragon did not speak.
She did not thank anyone, did not nod, did not return a brass button or a handless watch from her hoard, and did not produce a compass from anywhere.

She lowered her head, touched her snout once to the hatchling's damp back, and then folded her wing over it completely, a great taut curtain of it, until only a small wet head peeked out between the feathers of her edge.
The storm had not stopped.
The waves still boomed against the grate below, and the wind still tore at the broken window, and the lighthouse still drummed like a struck barrel.
But the upper room was dry, and the door was still just a door.
They went out the way they'd come in — along the coastal path, above the seaweed line, the safe way Duru had shown her.
When the path forked at the steep slope, Duru said, "Left here, above the black rocks," and Ekin turned left without a word, without checking the slope first, without needing to.
Duru, for her part, said nothing about the compass at all.
Nothing about the nest, or the lunging, or the sea.
The loss sat between them, acknowledged, unmocked, and that was its own strange kindness.
By the time they came down into the harbor, the fishermen were restacking their scattered papers and the sky had gone the color of wet slate.
Somewhere behind them, up on the headland, the storm went on without them.

Ekin's hand went to her pocket out of habit, into the space where the compass should have been — and found only the cord, the empty brass cord with its little clasp, which had somehow stayed looped through her belt loop when everything else had been swept away.
She didn't hide it.
She didn't tuck it away or pretend it wasn't there.
She stood at the harbor wall for a moment, turning the empty cord slowly around her finger, feeling how light it was and how heavy.
Then she ran three quick steps and caught up with Duru, walking side by side into the wind.

approved_plan.reader_promise:
12 yaş okuru; fantastik kıyı macerası; önce İngilizce yazım için 1.400–1.800
kelimelik hedef önerisi. Merak, sürtüşmeli ortaklık ve kaybı inkâr etmeyen bir son.
Başlangıç sorusu: Ekin dedesinin pusulasını geri alabilecek mi? Asıl çatışma:
Ekin kendi hatası ortaya çıktığında sorumluluk alabilecek mi?

Pusula büyülü değildir. Hazine, kehanet veya büyük Saga sırrı açıklamaz. Bu tek
bölümün kendi macerası kapanır; devam bölümü gerektiren yapay cliffhanger yoktur.
approved_plan.mock_context:
**Ekin:** On iki yaşında bir kız. Meraklı, çabuk karar veriyor; kendisine yol
gösterilmesini küçümsenmek gibi algılıyor. Dedesiyle yaptığı kıyı gezilerinden
kalan pirinç pusula, o gezileri tek başına da yapabileceğine dair kişisel bir
hatıra. Dedenin öldüğü varsayılmayacak; hikâye bir yas anlatısına dönüştürülmeyecek.

**Duru:** Ekin'in yaşıtı. Eski fenerin yolunu biliyor. Ekin'e hizmet eden kusursuz
yardımcı değil: laf sokuyor, merakını bazen saklıyor, kendi fikrinin dinlenmesini
istiyor. Fenerin kapısı uzun süredir ilk kez açık olduğu için o da içeri girmek
istiyor. Ortaklıklarının başlangıç nedeni yalnızca Ekin'e iyilik etmek değil.

**Anne deniz ejderhası:** Çocukların beline yaklaşan, geniş gövdeli bir hayvan;
diğer ejderhalara göre küçük. Uçabilir, küçük bir metal nesneyi taşıyabilir.
Konuşmaz, büyü yapmaz, insan niyetini okuyamaz. Yuvaya parlak eşyalar taşır.
İnsanlara saldırma amacı yok; yaklaşanı kanat açıp tıslayarak uzaklaştırır.

**Yavru:** Kedi büyüklüğünde, koşabilir ve dar aralıklara girebilir; henüz
uçamaz. Düşüp yaralanması veya grafik acı tasviri yok. Korktuğunda dar, karanlık
bir yere saklanma davranışı var. Annenin ganimetleriyle ilgilenmesi keşifte görülür.

**Başlangıç eşyaları:** Ekin'in pusulası ve ceketi; Duru'nun sıradan giysileri.
Sonradan ip, kanca, kesici alet, özel ışık veya kurtarma ekipmanı belirmeyecek.
approved_plan.setting_and_hazards:
Fener ana karaya bağlı bir burunda. Limandan üst kapıya çıkan kıyı patikası su
basma çizgisinin üstünde; bir ada geçidi, kopacak köprü veya gizli ikinci yol yok.
Gidişte Duru korunaklı patikayı gösterir. Fırtına yaklaşır ama başlangıçta dalgalar
alt deniz duvarına dahi ulaşmaz; çocuklar kısa bir ziyaret yapabileceklerini sanır.

Üst giriş odası kuru ve gün ışığı alıyor. Anne burada, geniş kırık pencereden
ulaşabildiği köşede yuva kurmuş. Odanın bir kenarından alt bakım odasına dar,
dönüşlü bir insan merdiveni iner. Çocuklar geçebilir; annenin geniş göğsü dönüşten
geçemez. Bu engel sahnede annenin gerçekten denemesiyle görünür; sonradan ilan
edilen bir tür kuralı değildir.

Alt bakım odasının denize bakan açıklığında sabit bir demir ızgara vardır. Su
ve küçük nesneler geçebilir; anne dışarıdan buraya giremez. Fırtınada dalgalar
bu açıklıktan içeri dolar. İç merdiven üstteki kuru odaya çıkar ve sağlam kalır.
Çocuklar yüzmeye, dalmaya veya görünmeyen zeminde ilerlemeyecek.

Tehlike tüm binanın birden batması değil: alt odanın yavru için hızla güvensiz
olması, görüşü bozan su ve dışarıdaki rüzgârın artmasıdır. Fırtına aniden durmaz;
sonda annenin uçması gerekmeyecek. Anne ve yavru kuru üst odada buluşur.

scenes.title: Limandaki hırsızlık
scenes.approved_action:
Ekin pusulaya bakarken ejderha onu kapar. Hayvanın kanadı tezgâhtaki hafif
kâğıtları savurur; hırsızlık kısa, canlı bir sahnedir. Ekin peşinden koşar.
Duru onun yanlış yöne gittiğini söyleyip fenerin penceresindeki parıltıyı gösterir.
scenes.required_end_state: Pusula anne ejderhada; iki çocuk limanda, birlikte gitmeye karar verir.

scenes.title: İstemeden ortaklık
scenes.approved_action:
Duru kıyı patikasını seçer. Ekin daha kısa gördüğü taşlık kıyıya yönelmek ister;
Duru dalgaların oraya kadar çıkacağını gösterir. Ekin onun yolunu isteksizce kabul
eder. Aralarında birinin sürekli haklı olduğu ders sahnesi değil, karşılıklı
iğnelemeler ve fener hakkında ortak merak vardır. Açık kapıdan içeri girerler.
scenes.required_end_state: İkisi kuru üst odada. Geri dönüş yolu okura gösterilmiş olur.

scenes.title: Hırsızın evi
scenes.approved_action:
Rüzgârın boş fenerde çıkardığı sesleri, tuzla matlaşmış camları ve yuvaya taşınmış
ufak parlak eşyaları keşfederler. Ekin pusulayı görür. Duru bir yavru fark eder
ve yaklaşmadan önce beklemelerini ister. Ekin her tıslamayı pusulasına karşı
bir meydan okuma gibi algılar; Duru'nun uyarısını emir sayar.

Dar merdiven ağzı ve alt odanın ızgarasından duyulan dalga sesi bu sahnede gösterilir.
Çıkıştaki kapı ve dönüş yolu kapanmaz. Anne çocuklarla yuvanın arasında durur.
scenes.required_end_state: Herkes üst odada, pusula yuvanın yanında. Yavru ile inişin yeri belli.

scenes.title: Ekin'in hatası
scenes.approved_action:
Ekin pusulaya hızla uzanır. Anne kanadını açarak onu uzaklaştırır. Pusula yuvanın
kenarından yuvarlanıp merdivenden alt odaya gider. Ürken yavru da merdivenin altına
kaçar; çocuklar onun nereye gittiğini görür. Anne peşinden inmeye çalışır ama dar
dönüşte kalır. Duru çocuğu veya hayvanı iterek sorunu büyütmez.

Ekin merdivenden bakarken bir dalga pusulayı ızgaranın aralığından denize sürükler.
Yavru alt basamakların yakınındaki kuru taş çıkıntıya çekilir. Suyu görürler;
tehlike anlatıcının soyut uyarısıyla değil sahnedeki değişimle belirginleşir.
scenes.required_end_state:
Pusula denizde ve erişilemiyor. Anne üstte; yavru altta. Çocuklar
merdivenin kuru bölümünde. Fenerin üst çıkışı hâlâ kullanılabilir.

scenes.title: Geri dönmek yerine sorumluluk almak
scenes.approved_action:
Ekin önce gözünü pusulanın kaybolduğu ızgaradan ayıramaz. Duru gitmeleri gerektiğini
söyler; ardından yavrunun su yükseldikçe geri çekildiğini görürler. Ekin hayvanı
kendisinin ürküttüğünü kabul eder ve Duru'dan yardım ister. Duru da ona kızgın
olmasına rağmen kalır. Karar: Kendi kaybına kapanıp ayrılmak mı, yol açtığı
tehlikeyi gidermek için güvenli kalan kısa fırsatı kullanmak mı?

Ekin kuru kalan basamakta çömelip ceketini açar. Yavrunun arkasına geçmez veya
onu suya doğru kovalamaz. Duru aynı merdivende bir üst basamakta durur; görüşü
izler ve Ekin'in ceketle aldığı yavruyu yukarı aktarırken destek olur. Yavru
ulaşılabilir taş çıkıntıdadır; uçuruma atlama, suya dalma veya yeni büyü yoktur.
Ekin ardından aynı basamaklardan çıkar. Yazım bu basit eylemi sayfalar süren bir
mekanik bulmacaya çevirmemeli; gerilim Ekin'in tereddüdü ve hayvanın korkusundadır.
scenes.required_end_state: Çocuklar ve yavru kuru üst odada; anneyle buluşurlar. Pusula hâlâ kayıp.

scenes.title: Pusulasız dönüş
scenes.approved_action:
Ekin yavruyu annesinin yanına bırakır. Anne kanadını yavrunun üstüne kapatır;
konuşup teşekkür etmez, pusulayı veya başka bir armağanı geri vermez. Duru ile
Ekin gidişte gördüğümüz patikadan eve döner. Ekin bu kez Duru'nun yönlendirmesini
itiraz etmeden dinler; Duru da kaybıyla alay etmez.
scenes.required_end_state:
Ekin pusulaya olanları saklamamaya karar verir. Son görüntü: cebindeki boş pusula
kordonunu parmaklarıyla çevirirken Duru'ya yetişmesi. Mutlu bir kahkaha her şeyi
silmez; okur hem kaybı hem aralarındaki değişimi hisseder. Tamamlanan macera
yalnızca 'bir ders öğrendi' cümlesiyle özetlenmez.

spans: Ekin had been waiting all morning for the clouds to thin enough to read the sky, but the brass compass in her hands didn't care about clouds.
Its needle swung once, steadied, and pointed her straight along the harbor wall toward the headland where the old lighthouse stood.
Her grandfather had pressed it into her palm at the end of last summer, with the promise that she could come back and walk the coast on her own.
This was supposed to be that walk.
The shadow crossed her before she heard the wings.
It dropped out of the low grey sky like a thrown cloak — a sea dragon, smaller than the ones fishermen grumbled about, but broad across the chest, with wings that caught the wind and snapped taut.
Its claws closed around the compass cord, wrenched it free of her fingers, and beat upward in a single heavy stroke.
The downdraft scattered a fishmonger's paperwork across the wet cobbles, and someone shouted as a stack of receipts swirled into the harbor.
"My compass!" Ekin was already running, boots skidding on the slick stones.
The dragon didn't even look back.
It rose over the roofs, banked once, and glided toward the headland.
Ekin cut left, toward the cliff steps that climbed the fastest way up, but a hand caught her sleeve.
"Not that way." A girl her own age stood there, dark hair whipped across her face, pointing with her chin.
See?" In the lighthouse's highest window, something small and brass flashed once in the grey light.
"Duru," the girl added, as if that explained everything.
Ekin yanked her sleeve back, ready to argue, then looked at the cliff steps, at the wind flattening the grass up there, at the flash in the window again.
She wasn't leaving it in a dragon's nest.
The coastal path left the harbor through a gap in the sea wall and climbed gently along the spine of the headland, well above the tideline.
Duru walked it like she'd been born on it, stepping over the loose stones without looking down.
Ekin lasted about two hundred paces before the shortcut tempted her.
"There." She pointed down the slope, where a rocky shelf of ledges angled toward the lighthouse's base.
She stopped, crouched, and laid her palm flat on a dark stone near the path's edge.
The wind's turned, and when it turns, the swell comes up over those rocks." She nodded at a line of dried seaweed clinging to the boulders well above the water.
"The sea left that there this morning.
You want to be standing under it when the next wave remembers?"
The waves were still slapping harmlessly against the lower sea wall, but the seaweed told a different story, and the wind was rising in longer, colder pulls.
She hated being told what to do — hated it most when the person telling her was right.
"My path," Duru agreed, without any gloating in it, which somehow made it worse and better at the same time.
Below them the harbor shrank to a scatter of masts; above them the lighthouse grew, its white paint gone grey and scabbed with salt.
Ekin had never been this close.
"Is it really empty?" she asked, breathing harder than she wanted to admit.
"Everyone says it's been shut for years."
"Empty —" She stopped at the bend where the path met the flat ground of the headland, and stared.
The lighthouse's upper door stood open.
Not broken, not hanging off its hinges — just open, wide and dark, the first time in living memory.
"Nobody opens that door," Duru said quietly, and for the first time since the harbor, her voice carried no teasing at all.
Whatever had stolen Ekin's compass had also opened a door that nobody opened, and neither of them could walk past that.
Duru followed, and pulled the door shut behind them against the rising wind — not locked, just closed, the way they'd found the way back clearly marked by the path outside the window.
The room they stepped into was dry and tall, lit by a wide window on the seaward side whose glass had long ago cracked and fallen away, leaving a jagged, generous opening to the sky.
And in that opening, folding her wings like a ship coming to anchor, was the thief.
The mother dragon was smaller than the stories claimed sea dragons were, but she filled the corner of the room the way a boat fills a boathouse.

She had woven her nest into the crushed shadow of the broken window out of whatever the sea and the wind had offered: coiled rope, torn fishing net, dried kelp, and — gleaming through it all like coins at the bottom of a well — a hoard of small bright things.
A pocket watch with no hands.
And there, resting on the very edge of the pile, its glass face catching the grey daylight: the compass.
"Wait." Duru's hand came out, not grabbing, just open, like a fence.
Her eyes weren't on the nest.
They were on the shadows behind it, where a shape the size of a large cat had uncurled — a hatchling, all oversized flippers and wet down, watching them with round dark eyes.
It wasn't a roar, nothing dramatic — just a long, dry, razor sound, and her wings half-opened, shading the nest like a drawn curtain.
Between the children and the pile of treasure, she had settled herself like a wall.
Ekin heard the hiss and felt it land on her like a dare.
My grandfather's compass.* Every sound the dragon made seemed to say *no*, and every *no* made Ekin's jaw set harder.
"I'm not telling you what to do.
The wind moaned through the broken window, and beneath it, from somewhere below the floor, came another sound — rhythmic, heavy, hollow.
Ekin glanced around and saw it: a narrow staircase spiraling down into the lighthouse's belly, human-sized, tight and turning, its stone steps worn smooth in the middle.
The wave-sound rose from down there, muffled and enormous, the noise of the sea hitting something fixed and iron.
"There's a grate down there, open to the water.
This whole tower is a drum in a storm."
"Then we take the compass and go," Ekin whispered back, eyes fixed on the brass flash at the nest's edge.
The hatchling peeked around her flank.

The waves boomed below, and the wind tore at the broken window, and the door behind them stayed exactly where they'd left it — shut, but not locked, the path home plain through the dry daylight outside.
That was the thing she would turn over later, walking home — there had been no plan, just the compass sitting three steps away in a pile of stolen junk, and her hand already moving.
"I'm just taking what's mine," she said, and lunged.
The mother dragon moved faster than anything that broad had a right to.
One wing snapped out, thick as a sail, and swept the air between them.
Ekin flinched back — and the wind of the wing's passage, or the drag of her sleeve, or simply the whole room flinching with her, knocked the compass off the nest's edge.
It hit the floor with a brass clatter and rolled.

Ekin dove, missed, and watched it spin in a widening arc across the floorboards, past her fingers, over the lip of the stairwell opening, and down — a shrinking spiral of flashing brass, ticking against every worn step, down and down into the drumming dark.
The hatchling shrieked — a thin, uncanny sound — and bolted after it, flippers scrabbling, vanishing down the same stairs in three bounds.
The mother roared and threw herself at the stairwell.

It was that simple and that terrible: her shoulders jammed against the curved stone at the first turn, her wings pinned half-folded, her claws scrabbling on rock as she heaved and wedged and could not pass.
She backed out, hissing, jammed herself in again, and got no further.
"I see it." Duru was flat on her stomach at the stairwell's lip, peering down.
There's a ledge — the little one's near it —" Then her face changed.
Far below, through the lower room's seaward opening, she could see it: a fixed iron grate, bars thick as her wrist, and beyond the bars the grey sea heaving.
A wave struck the grate and burst through it, not as spray but as a whole moving wall, sweeping across the lower floor, slamming against the stair's stone base.
And when it drained back, the compass went with it — a small bright tumble through the bars, out into the churn, gone.
The sea stared back, grey and vast and absolutely uninterested.
The hatchling, washed and terrified, hauled itself out of the reach of the next wave onto a dry stone ledge near the bottom of the stairs, pressed itself against the wall, and made itself small.
Above, its mother thrashed once more against the stone turn of the stairwell, felt the shape of the passage with her snout, and went still — stuck on the wrong side of her own child's hiding place.
Ekin couldn't look away from the grate.
The compass was down there — *had been* down there — and some stubborn part of her kept waiting for the sea to give it back, for a wave to set it gently on the stones like an apology.
"We have to go." Duru was on her feet.
This room — the whole bottom of the tower —"
"I know." Ekin's voice came out flat.
Her grandfather's compass, given with a promise, swallowed by the sea in front of her own eyes because she had lunged at a dragon's nest without thinking.
She was looking down the stairs again.
The water had reached the base of the ledge.

The hatchling had retreated to the last dry handspan of stone and stood there shivering, too frightened to climb the steps toward the huge stuck shape of its mother, too crowded by the rising wash to stay.
Ekin looked at the lost compass.
The choice arranged itself with brutal clarity: she could walk out the door with Duru right now and grieve properly, or she could go down those stairs and fix the thing she had broken.
"I scared it down there," she said.
"It ran because of me." She swallowed.
Duru looked at her for a long second — angry, Ekin could see, genuinely angry, and staying anyway.
"The ledge holds for now," Duru said.
"The steps above the wet line are dry.
Ekin went down, step by careful step, on the dry upper stairs.
At the level of the ledge she crouched, slowly, and opened her jacket, holding one side out like a sling.
The hatchling hissed, a tiny copy of its mother's sound, and pressed harder into the corner.
"I'm not going to chase you into the water," Ekin said.
"I already did enough." She stayed exactly where she was, coat open, hand out, and waited.
The hatchling's round eyes fixed on her.
Below, the sea drew back for the next wave.
The hatchling took one shuffle-step toward her.
Whether it was the cold, the noise, or the open coat that looked more like a nest than anything else in the tower, Ekin never asked.

At the last moment, as the roar of the incoming wave filled the lower room, Ekin scooped — gently, under the belly, the way you'd lift a stray cat — and tucked the hatchling against her chest inside the jacket just as the water exploded against the grate below the ledge and swirled over the stone where it had been standing.
"Go!" Duru pulled her by the shoulder as she came up.

Step by step, Ekin climbed, the hatchling a warm trembling weight against her ribs, Duru a half-flight above her calling out the dry steps, until they spilled together into the dry upper room, sea-damp and shaking, and Ekin knelt and let the hatchling spill out of her coat onto the floorboards.
The mother dragon was off the stairwell and across the room before it finished righting itself.

Ekin picked the hatchling up one last time — it had gone strangely still, watching its mother's face — and carried it the last few steps, setting it down right at the edge of the nest, close enough to touch.
The mother dragon did not speak.
She did not thank anyone, did not nod, did not return a brass button or a handless watch from her hoard, and did not produce a compass from anywhere.

She lowered her head, touched her snout once to the hatchling's damp back, and then folded her wing over it completely, a great taut curtain of it, until only a small wet head peeked out between the feathers of her edge.
The waves still boomed against the grate below, and the wind still tore at the broken window, and the lighthouse still drummed like a struck barrel.
But the upper room was dry, and the door was still just a door.
They went out the way they'd come in — along the coastal path, above the seaweed line, the safe way Duru had shown her.
When the path forked at the steep slope, Duru said, "Left here, above the black rocks," and Ekin turned left without a word, without checking the slope first, without needing to.
Duru, for her part, said nothing about the compass at all.
Nothing about the nest, or the lunging, or the sea.
The loss sat between them, acknowledged, unmocked, and that was its own strange kindness.
By the time they came down into the harbor, the fishermen were restacking their scattered papers and the sky had gone the color of wet slate.
Somewhere behind them, up on the headland, the storm went on without them.

Ekin's hand went to her pocket out of habit, into the space where the compass should have been — and found only the cord, the empty brass cord with its little clasp, which had somehow stayed looped through her belt loop when everything else had been swept away.
She didn't tuck it away or pretend it wasn't there.
She stood at the harbor wall for a moment, turning the empty cord slowly around her finger, feeling how light it was and how heavy.
Then she ran three quick steps and caught up with Duru, walking side by side into the wind.
